column1: Mimicking

Can you describe the smelliest person you have met? My earliest recollection of an encounter with truly offensive body odor was when I was a young lad, barely into my teens. I was at a 4-H camp, a tradition in Trinidad and Tobago, a rite of passage for many of us impressionable youngsters. The sun blazed mercilessly, as it generally does in the tropics, and the air hung thick with the promise of a humid afternoon. Located in the northern part of the island, the camp comprised a mishmash of concrete buildings, a tired old football field, and a scattering of mango trees. My bunkmate, a fellow named Neville, was the culprit. Neville was, to put it mildly, a creature of habit, a trait that manifested in his hygiene, or rather, the distinct lack thereof. He possessed a singular aversion to the weekly ritual of showering, a fact that quickly became apparent to everyone in our shared dormitory.

What’s the most unprofessional thing a doctor has said to you? I once had a rather unfortunate encounter with a doctor, or rather, a specialist, who quite frankly, should have had their license revoked. I was enduring a particularly nasty bout of the flu and, after a week of enduring various over-the-counter remedies and home-grown concoctions, I decided to seek professional help and visit a clinic. I was met by a doctor who, from the moment they walked into the examination room, seemed utterly disinterested. The exam was conducted mechanically, with the doctor displaying minimal enthusiasm. After what felt like a cursory once-over, they sat down opposite me, tapping their pen on the desk with an air of impatience. ‘You got the flu,’ they stated matter-of-factly. 'I can give you a shot to make the symptoms more bearable'. Fair enough. They proceeded to prescribe some medication, but not before delivering a truly astonishing piece of unprofessional commentary. "Honestly," they said, "if my patients took better care of themselves, I wouldn't have to deal with this." They rolled their eyes. I was taken aback; never in my life had I encountered such a blatant lack of empathy or professional decorum. It was apparent that they viewed me, and perhaps all, patients as an irritating nuisance. I thought about how the Hippocratic Oath had completely eluded this doctor. As I took my leave, I couldn't help but feel a sense of resentment and disappointment. I mean, it's one thing to face a medical professional with a bad day, but another to encounter such a crass and dismissive attitude. It was a stark illustration that the provision of medical care is not always synonymous with compassion and understanding. Moreover, the doctor’s words suggested a deeper issue - an unwillingness to accept that their role entailed helping people who are unwell, not just lecturing them. That day I learned, the extent to which an individual's lack of professionalism can severely damage the patient-doctor dynamic.

Why do women *hate* nerdy men? This question, I believe, should be flipped on its head a bit. It's not that women universally *hate* nerdy men, per se. The word “hate” is typically quite a strong word and I believe that there are far more complex dynamics at play here than a simple blanket term can explain. What we can probably say with more accuracy is that many women do not find nerdy men attractive. Whether this is due to nature, nurture, or both, it's tough to say. The idea that there is a singular mold of ideal masculine behavior that all men should attempt to resemble I think is absolute gibberish. From observing the world around me as well as reading many a post on this site, it looks like a very wide array of males attracts women. This is not exactly news, but the actual reasons tend to differ and sometimes defy any semblance of logic. However, when we ask about why women are turned off, we enter into more promising territory, where some real answers may be derived.

What movies have you judged just by looking at their posters? I've been known to be a bit of a film snob, I'll freely admit it. I'm not proud of it, but I'll also confess that I've often formed a snap judgement about a movie based solely on its poster. And let's be clear, in a world of digital streaming and endless content, a poster is often the first impression a film gets to make. It's a visual sales pitch, and some are evidently more persuasive than others. The truly awful offenders I tend to steer away from, but there is a whole different category of posters that spark my intrigue. Those that come off as either ridiculously pretentious or incredibly derivative. For instance, I've always been skeptical of movies with minimalistic posters. You know the kind. A single object, a stark background, and maybe a cryptic title. These posters often scream high art and "we're too good for commercial appeal.” Now, I'm not necessarily against artistic expression, but these types of posters often feel a little too self-important, as if the filmmakers believe the sheer weight of their artistic vision is enough to carry the film. Then there are those posters that are essentially a collage of well-known actors' faces plastered near each other. It’s as if the film is begging you to believe it is worthy of your time. These types are not always bad movies, mind you, but they often feel like a product of the studio machine, designed for mass appeal, not for genuine artistic merit.

What is the lowest probability event you have personally witnessed? It may sound a bit dramatic, but for me, it involves the sudden and unexpected passing of someone I knew. This individual, who I'll refer to as "Mark," was the picture of vitality. He was a strapping, athletic man, maybe a few years older than me, and seemed the epitome of health. A regular at the local gym, Mark was a fitness fanatic, always pushing himself and encouraging others. He was jovial, friendly, and had this infectious zest for life that everyone around him admired. I remember seeing him just a few weeks before the event. We were at a community barbecue, and he was effortlessly charming, laughing with a group of friends and colleagues. He looked the picture of health, tanned from the sun and brimming with energy. He was the last person you’d expect to experience something so…final.The news reached me via a mutual acquaintance, and it was so utterly out of the blue, so completely improbable, that for a moment, I refused to believe it. The circumstances were vague initially, a sudden and inexplicable health complication. My brain struggled to process the information. It felt as though the fabric of reality had momentarily torn. Here was a man who seemed indestructible, extinguished in the blink of an eye. It was a harsh reminder of the fragility of existence, how quickly the rug can be pulled out from under you. It really shook me and I remember becoming profoundly affected by a wave of dread, not of death itself, but of the randomness of it all. It felt like a cosmic joke, a twist of fate that defied all logic and reason.

What's your take on Imane Khelif, a biologically proven male boxer, taking part in the Women's Boxing event at the Paris Olympics 2024? The ongoing debate surrounding Imane Khelif's eligibility for the women's boxing event at the Paris Olympics 2024 is, undeniably, a thorny issue. On one hand, we have the principles of inclusivity and fair play that underpin the Olympic spirit. To exclude someone based on their biological makeup, particularly when they've demonstrably striven to compete, seems, at its core, discriminatory. It's a sentiment that aligns with the evolving understanding of gender and identity in the modern world, a world where lines are blurring and the very definitions of "male" and "female" are being challenged, and in many cases, redefined. Furthermore, there's the matter of Khelif's individual journey, the dedication, and the sacrifices she's undoubtedly made to reach the pinnacle of her sport. Denying her the opportunity to compete on the world stage, after all that effort, would be a cruel blow. However, we cannot simply sweep aside the counter-arguments, the very legitimate concerns regarding the physical advantages a biological male might possess in a sport like boxing. The argument of a man's advantage is not merely limited to strength alone. Skeletal structure, muscle composition, and even cardiovascular capacity can all be contributing factors and this is very important when the competition is between the best of the best. These factors are not easily overcome, even through the strictest hormone treatments. This is more than simply a sporting contest; it is a competition where physical safety is of paramount importance, and one must be extra cautious. If such advantages are present, it could potentially put female competitors at increased risk of serious injury or, at the very minimum, provide an unfair competitive advantage. The organizers of these Olympics therefore seem to be treading a very fine line between these competing considerations. At times it's not clear whether they are leaning too heavily in one direction or the other, whether the considerations of inclusivity are coming at the cost of fair competition or the safety of others. This complex balancing act underscores the need for a clear, comprehensive, consistent, and universally accepted framework for categorizing competitors. This framework should, at the very least, take into account both the individual's rights and the overall integrity and fairness of the sport.

Has your friend ever saved your life? I've never been the sort to find myself in death-defying predicaments, so, thankfully, I've yet to owe my life to any of my friends. Though, I've often pondered the notion of a life-saving scenario and the myriad of possibilities that may come with it. Perhaps a daring rescue from a burning building, thwarting a mugging in the dark alleys of Port of Spain, or even a quick-thinking intervention during a medical emergency—the stuff of action movies and dramatic memoirs. Unfortunately, my reality has been rather bereft of such extraordinary circumstances, and the most danger I've faced involved the usual teenage recklessness.

Have you ever had a life-changing experience while working in fast food? As a teenager, I certainly spent a good amount of time slaving away in the fast food industry. During those formative years, I flipped burgers, mopped floors, and dealt with the occasional unruly customer, all while trying to save enough money to buy a beat-up jalopy. While the job itself was hardly glamorous, it did provide some valuable life lessons. But, a life-changing experience? That's a rather lofty claim for a job that mostly involved deep-frying things and yelling "Welcome to [Restaurant Name]!"That all changed on one particular Tuesday. The restaurant was packed with a lunchtime rush, and the crew was in full panic mode. Orders were piling up, the soda machine was spewing foam, and the fry baskets seemed to be in perpetual motion. Amidst the chaos, a frail elderly woman cautiously approached the counter, clutching a tattered purse and sporting a bewildered expression. She fumbled through the menu, her eyes struggling to focus on the bright, colourful pictures. She clearly wasn't accustomed to ordering in a fast-paced environment. The cashier, a surly young man with a piercing glare and a penchant for rolling his eyes, gestured impatiently for her to hurry up. My patience was also starting to wear too. "What'll it be, lady?" he barked.I was, for some reason, struck by something in her expression, something beyond the obvious befuddlement. There was a certain fragility, a quiet dignity in her posture, that stirred something within me. I decided to step in.  "Take your time, ma'am," I said gently, giving the cashier a look filled with warning. "We're not going anywhere.” I was taken aback by his unexpected quietness. She seemed startled, giving us both a wary look, but eventually managed to point at a picture of a burger. "That one," she croaked.

What are some bad movies that could have worked by just having a better screenplay? Many a cinematic catastrophe could have been averted, I reckon, with a solid, well-crafted screenplay. Take, for instance, the plethora of sci-fi flicks that squander their potential on nonsensical plots and convoluted dialogue. Picture this: a dazzling spaceship hurtling through the cosmos, state-of-the-art special effects, charismatic actors, all brought to a halt by a script riddled with plot holes deeper than space itself. One could almost visualize the director wringing his hands in despair as he watches his investment crumble into oblivion. Or consider the romantic comedies, so often choked by clichés and predictable storylines. A genuinely funny, original script could transform these into sparkling gems, breathing life into characters bogged down by tired tropes. Take note of the numerous action movies that suffer from a reliance on explosions and bravado at the expense of character depth and meaningful interactions. A tighter narrative, with less emphasis on gratuitous violence and more on compelling narratives, would have the potential to elevate such films from mindless entertainment to genuinely gripping experiences.

What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history? The only answer I can truly think of is the ending of *2001: A Space Odyssey*. I went into the film with a clear expectation of high-octane space battles or maybe a dramatic confrontation with the sentient HAL9000, the AI aboard the Discovery One. Instead, I was greeted with a cosmic light show, a psychedelic descent through the cosmos, and then...a fetus in orbit. Honestly, I was dumbfounded. Coming out of the cinema, I felt like I'd been given an intellectual puzzle box with the key permanently lost. I’d spent hours poring over theories and interpretations, trying to get some sense of resolution, some sort of clarification. However, the ending remains a complete enigma, a surreal and rather perplexing conclusion to a film that I had fully anticipated would deliver some kind of concrete answer to the questions it originally posed. The film is a masterpiece in its own right, but the ending is one giant head scratcher, a big cinematic letdown. The whole thing felt as though Stanley Kubrick was trying to troll his audience.

What’s your favorite movie based on true events? Hands down, it's "Catch Me If You Can". The film’s a captivating blend of fact and fiction, peppered with a good dose of Hollywood artistry which makes it all the more enthralling. The story of Frank Abagnale Jr., is already a cinematic goldmine. A young man who masterfully impersonates a doctor, a lawyer, and a pilot all while expertly scamming banks and forging checks. The sheer audacity of his exploits, coupled with his ability to constantly evade capture, provides ample fodder for a gripping narrative. The director, Steven Spielberg, skillfully transforms the story into a visually stunning and emotionally resonant piece of work. Leonardo DiCaprio's portrayal of Abagnale is simply superb, capturing both the mischievous charm and the underlying vulnerability of the character. The film also benefits from a stellar supporting cast, with Tom Hanks playing the determined FBI agent who makes it his personal mission to bring Abagnale to justice. The cat-and-mouse game between them is one of the movie’s greatest strengths, filled with suspense, wit, and, surprisingly, moments of camaraderie and respect. What I really love about "Catch Me If You Can", especially as a movie that is based on a true story, is the way the human element is explored. It dives into Abagnale's motivations, exploring the reasons behind his deceptive actions and the emotional impact his choices have on himself and others. The film doesn't shy away from the consequences of his actions, subtly weaving in themes of loneliness, guilt, and the search for identity. It is precisely this exploration that elevates the movie beyond a simple crime thriller into a complex character study. As a sidenote, I can recall watching this movie on the same day as another Spielberg classic: the animated "The Adventures of Tintin".

As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something? During my tenure as a teacher’s assistant at the University of the West Indies, a rather unusual accusation was levied against me. It occurred not in the hallowed halls of academia, but rather, within the raucous confines of a university fete. I was, as I still am, rather fond of a good lime, and as fate would have it, I found myself at this particular shindig, enjoying the festivities alongside some fellow students. It was a lively affair, replete with the melodious strains of soca and the intoxicating aroma of street food. Amidst the revelry, I was approached by a group of students, their faces etched with a mixture of bewilderment and accusation. The charge? That I, in some clandestine manner, had been tampering with the university's library database, ensuring that the most coveted textbooks were consistently unavailable when they needed them most. The absurdity of the situation was not lost on me. My academic repertoire leaned more toward philosophical musings than digital skullduggery. I was a student of philosophy, not a hacker! I explained with what patience I could muster that I was as flummoxed as they were, and had no involvement in any such digital shenanigans. Alas, like all good rumour, it wasn't long before the accusations died down, another example of the strange confluence of circumstances that sometimes manifest in the unpredictable theatre of life.

Why do some people not like Coldplay? Coldplay, for a band that has dominated the airwaves for the better part of two decades, appears to be a peculiar paradox. Their music, a blend of melancholic piano chords, arena-rock anthems, and Chris Martin's distinctive vocals, has garnered them a massive global following, chart-topping albums, and countless accolades. Yet, amidst all this success, there exists a vocal minority who vehemently dislike them. It's a curious phenomenon, really, and one that can be dissected from various angles.One frequent criticism leveled at Coldplay is their perceived predictability. Their sound, while undeniably polished and well-produced, sometimes veers into the territory of the formulaic. Critics often accuse them of rehashing the same themes of love, loss, and longing, albeit with incrementally different musical arrangements. This can lead to a sense of musical fatigue, particularly for listeners who crave more innovation or sonic experimentation. Essentially, once you’ve heard one Coldplay song, the argument goes, you’ve heard them all. There isn't a whole lot of space for improvisation even though they are extremely talented musicians.

What show / movie had no right to be as good as it was? I'm tempted to say *The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air*. It was supposed to be a frivolous sitcom starring a rapper. Yet it became an insightful, funny, and, dare I say, educational show that tackled serious issues with a level of gravitas rarely seen in its genre. I remember watching it as a child and finding myself genuinely moved by the storyline and the characters, far more than I had any right to be. I recall scenes that discussed racial profiling, police brutality, and the challenges faced by young Black men in America with a nuance that belied the show's comedic origins. The theme song, a catchy tune detailing Will Smith's move from Philadelphia to Bel-Air, remains iconic and instantly brings back fond memories. The show's success wasn't just about the witty banter or the over-the-top antics of Uncle Phil and Carlton; it was about the heart and the underlying message of family, perseverance, and the importance of staying true to yourself. It was a triumph of storytelling and an impressive display of both the power of comedy and the potential for it to touch upon the deeper complexities of the human experience. *Fresh Prince* went on to become, for me, a staple of my childhood; a feel-good show that taught me the value of laughter, loyalty and the importance of a good, strong, close-knit family.

Which actor played a villain role too well for comfort? Heath Ledger as The Joker. I’ll never get tired of saying that. He was the right actor, at the right time and clearly the right script. When I first saw *The Dark Knight*, I was simply blown away. At first, I wasn't even sure he was the Joker. I knew of Heath Ledger and remembered him as that cute guy in *10 things I hate about you*. I'd seen him in other roles and hadn't been particularly impressed. He was never an actor whom I particularly took note of but here he was, transformed. I'm pretty sure my jaw must’ve dropped at the very moment he appeared from the shadows during the bank robbery. I was a kid again. I’m not sure I’ve ever been so engrossed in a character’s appearance on screen. The way he spoke, his cadence, his mannerisms. He was the most terrifying, yet captivating character I'd ever seen portrayed. The fact that he was a villain, and so supremely a dangerous one made it all the more intriguing. Every time the Joker appeared, I was on the edge of my seat. He was so unpredictable. You didn’t know whether you should laugh or be terrified. His performance was so mesmerising that even though Batman was the hero, I was more interested in the villan. He was a force of nature. The only thing more impressive than his masterful performance was the fact that it came from a man who was only in his late twenties at the time. The word ‘genius’ has always been a bit of an overrated platitude in my book but if there was ever a time when that word could be applied, it would be for Heath Ledger, the Joker. It was and is a truly iconic performance.

What things do people say that make you roll your eyes? There's a certain brand of pronouncements that, upon hearing, automatically triggers an involuntary eye roll from me. Statements that are simply, unequivocally, and undeniably *obvious*. I'm talking about those pearls of wisdom that are less revelations and more a regurgitation of common knowledge dressed up like some profound insight - as if *that* warranted some deep, contemplative examination.Take, for instance, the classic, "You miss 100% of the shots you don't take." Oh, really? Is that how it works? I'd genuinely never have divined that unless someone had felt the need to spell it out for me. Or perhaps, "Treat others how you want to be treated." Groundbreaking stuff, I must say. One can almost hear the angels singing as some life-altering concept is unveiled. The audacity of such self-evident declarations always gets me; the speakers seem to assume they're imparting unprecedented truths. And it’s invariably delivered with utmost seriousness, as though they’re the founding fathers of common sense.Another one that gets me: “Everything happens for a reason.” The amount of times I've heard this trite cliché, particularly in the face of misfortune, is staggering. The unadulterated absurdity of using such a banal phrase to comfort someone, usually accompanied by a patronizing pat on the back – it really is an egregious and tiresome thing. It's like they're suggesting that the universe is meticulously orchestrating events for some convoluted, grand design we can't possibly fathom. Please. These platitudes are more often than not a lazy substitute for actually having a conversation or offering genuine empathy. They’re the verbal equivalent of a shrug, a way of putting on a show of caring without actually having to do anything. It’s the social equivalent of a get-out-of-jail-free card, a way of dismissing difficult sentiments with a conveniently packaged dose of lukewarm wisdom. And, as I mentioned, when I encounter such displays, my eyes automatically do that little spin. The real kicker? The people who utter these phrases usually don't even believe them. They just know it’s a thing people say to sound as though they are being, in any way, helpful.

What's the most ridiculous thing a coworker told on you to your boss for? One of the most asinine things a colleague ever did was file a complaint because she felt I was making her look bad. I worked at a finance company and for a couple of years, I occupied the role of middle management. Our team's collective performance was on an upward trajectory, surpassing even the loftiest of expectations. A new hire, let's call her Brenda, was assigned to our department. Now, Brenda was a peculiar character, somewhat lacking in tact and prone to bouts of extreme insecurity. She was the type who, if you complimented her on a dress, would immediately start talking about an alternative dress she felt was better. If you asked her how she was doing, she would go on for an hour about her ailments. The company’s strategy was to boost profits by targeting high-end clients. This meant a lot of outreach to ultra-wealthy individuals and families. Brenda took offense to this tactic, claiming that it was a betrayal and that we should target the poor and the middle class. At team meetings, when the goal was to discuss strategies to achieve the set targets, she would go on about the morality of high finance and how her work was going against her values. Her negativity could be rather frustrating but as a manager you just go with the flow, and keep everything productive. Brenda would continuously botch her tasks, resulting in numerous errors and setbacks. I, being her boss, was tasked with correcting and redoing most of her mistakes. Because she wasn't hitting her quotas she would often arrive late to meetings and be consistently absent and unproductive for large swathes of the day. I would document everything while providing her with guidance on how to improve her performance. I arranged several meetings with her to discuss her performance issues and give her the opportunity to put forth ideas as to how she could do better. All these efforts fell on deaf ears. My boss suggested that I give her another warning before we let her go. This is where the real fun and idiocy started. Brenda decided to go directly to my boss and complain that I was picking on her. She went on to embellish her situation, claiming I was constantly berating her in front of her coworkers and that I was attempting to undermine her standing in the company. At the company, all the managers are on their own and your performance is measured independently rather than by how the teams do on a broad context. Her complaint was met with a degree of cynicism but my boss was obligated to investigate. I was called in and had to defend myself against Brenda’s fabricated accusations. My reputation and credibility were somewhat damaged, although it was soon very obvious that Brenda was the problem. After a thorough investigation, during which it was revealed that Brenda had failed to meet her quotas, the company decided to let her go. Her exit was met with mixed feelings. Some were relieved, some felt bad. Everyone was glad for me. Her attempt to smear my name had backfired rather spectacularly. In the end, she was a lesson to us all. The real ridiculousness to all this, I always thought, was her audacity in attempting to shift the blame from her own lack of professionalism.

What red flag did you have right before a job offer that you wish you had heeded? I remember applying for a job at this company, a tech start-up that was buzzing with ambition and the promise of disrupting the industry. On paper, it looked ideal: an innovative culture, a competitive salary, and a chance to work on cutting-edge projects. The interview process was quite intense, involving multiple rounds and interactions with various team members. I was impressed with the energy and the obvious intelligence of the people I met. They were all young, driven, and passionate about their work. I felt like I was a great fit for the role and that my skillset perfectly aligned with the company's requirements. However, there was this one minor detail that I should have taken more seriously. During my final interview, I was taken on a tour of the office. I noticed that the office was a bit of a mess. Not just the usual cluttered desks, but empty pizza boxes, unwashed coffee mugs, and clothes thrown over chairs. Though I didn't pay it any mind at the time, there was a palpable undercurrent of stress emanating from the employees who were hunched over their computers, with some openly shouting at each other. There was also very little in the way of daylight, with the blinds drawn and the air thick with second-hand smoke. It was the sort of environment that was described back in the day as having the hallmarks of an all-night party. I dismissed it as signs that they were immersed in a critical task, or maybe it was just a very youthful company.

What is an unpopular opinion you hold? I've always found the whole hustle culture phenomenon to be a bit… off-putting, to say the least. This unrelenting pressure to be "productive," to always be "grinding," to treat every waking moment as an opportunity to maximize output – it just feels exhausting. Sure, I understand the value of hard work and ambition. I'm not advocating for sloth or complacency. But this current narrative, where every leisure activity must be framed as "self-care" or "personal development," where rest feels like a weakness to be conquered, it strikes me as deeply unhealthy. This constant need to optimize, to be the best, the most efficient, the most successful version of oneself, it can be detrimental to mental and physical well-being. The simple act of enjoying a sunset, reading a book, or spending time with loved ones for the pure pleasure of it – these things are often relegated to the margins, deemed less valuable than the next career move or side hustle. Don't get me wrong; wealth creation holds its own merits. I certainly would love more monetary resources. However, there's this prevailing idea that if you're not constantly striving, you're somehow falling behind, and that notion is utterly wrong. I believe that a balanced life, one that includes moments of genuine rest and enjoyment without guilt, is ultimately more conducive to long-term success and personal fulfillment. This "go-getter" mentality can often lead to burnout, depression, and a skewed perspective on what truly matters in life.

What is that one picture that describes the lowest point in your life? A while back I recall seeing this meme circulating the internet. It was a picture of a man sitting down looking completely forlorn and defeated with a rain cloud above his head. The meme was a humorous depiction of depression, but for a short while I could vividly recall the feeling of the lowest point in my life. It felt as though my soul became despondent and I was unable to escape these dark and somber feelings. I'm certain that I was experiencing a bout of depression. I didn't know what was happening to me. It was during the lockdown of 2020, I had recently been fired from my job, had a plethora of debts stacked up, my vehicle needed essential repairs, and I was cooped up in a dingy apartment all alone with little to no money to my name. I felt as though my life was in shambles, as though I was standing on the edge of a cliff, about to fall into an abyss of darkness. When I sought out and read up on the accounts of other people, I found that my issues weren't as bad as my own mind was making it out to be. Still, I felt as though nothing would get better, and that this would be an eternity of despair. I was a very social person who enjoyed the company of friends and family. But every single person I knew was far away from me. My phone would be silent for days on end, as I stared at the blank wall in front of me. In my mind there was nothing else that mattered in the world but my suffering. The picture would be me in that apartment, sitting in a chair, motionless, staring blankly at the wall.

Whom did you feel bad for in high school? In my adolescent years, I was something of a wallflower, observing the dramas and comedies of high school life from a distance. I wasn't particularly popular, nor was I particularly ostracized. I occupied that middle ground, just another face in the crowd. And it was this vantage point that allowed me to witness the subtle nuances of teenage tribulations. More often than not, it was the individuals perpetually stuck on the periphery, the ones who didn't quite fit in, who elicited a sense of empathy within me. I didn't necessarily feel "bad" for anyone out of a sense of pity. Rather, I simply understood their predicament. The social landscape of high school can be a brutal arena, rife with fleeting alliances, petty rivalries, and the constant pressure to conform to sometimes nonsensical norms. The quieter ones, those who shied away from the spotlight, often became targets, not of overt malice, but of an indifferent disregard, an invisibility that, in many ways, was crueler than any blatant act of bullying. I remember there was this chap, call him Mark, who was always alone, reading in the library, a book his constant companion. He harboured a gentle spirit, a genuine kindness that seemingly went unnoticed by everyone else. No one really bothered him, and he never caused trouble. It was as if he was simply not there. I always found myself wishing he had a friend, someone to share a laugh with, or simply someone to acknowledge him every once in a while. Then there was Jennifer, a girl who seemed out of place, dressing from a bygone era, always wearing long skirts. She tried hard to connect with others but often felt like an outsider, misunderstood and misjudged. I would witness girls whisper about her fashion choices behind their hands and there was always an uncomfortable awkwardness around her. It wasn’t necessarily a sense of pity that I felt for these individuals. It was more of a feeling of shared humanity, a recognition of the silent struggles that often went unnoticed, the quiet battles fought in the shadows of adolescence. These were the kind of people that I wish someone spoke up for them. I wasn't one to speak up, I was too shy. However, I think it is something everyone should do from time to time.

Which supporting actress was much more memorable than the star of a movie? This is a tricky one. I often find that in the annals of cinema, the supporting cast can sometimes outshine the leading lady, leaving a more indelible mark on the viewing public's collective consciousness. It's akin to a well-crafted side dish stealing the thunder from the main course. I'd have to cast my vote for Helena Bonham Carter, she is more memorable than the star in *Fight Club*. I remember watching that film as a teenager and, in my youthful and rather callow estimation, finding Edward Norton to be a rather bland and forgettable presence. Brad Pitt was, of course, exquisitely preening, but it was the delightfully unhinged and ever-so-slightly terrifying Marla Singer, brought to life by Bonham Carter, whose presence and quirky charm truly captured my attention. She was the unpredictable, chaotic element that kept the entire film afloat. Her performance wasn't just a supporting role; it was the chaotic counterpoint to the film’s inherent masculinity and machismo. And it wasn't just about appearance. Bonham Carter is a master of the craft, and she has the unique gift of making the outlandish real, the bizarre understandable and completely captivating. The star, I can barely recall, but the supporting role, ah, that's cinematic gold.

What is the scariest moment you have had in your own home? The most harrowing experience I've had within the confines of my abode occurred a few years ago. It was a typical Tuesday evening; the sun had already dipped below the horizon, casting long, eerie shadows across my living room. I was engrossed in a documentary on the telly, a rather somber affair detailing the migratory patterns of penguins. The volume was comfortably low and the only other sound was the gentle hum of the refrigerator. Suddenly, a bloodcurdling shriek pierced the tranquility. It erupted from the bedroom, a sound that sent a jolt of pure adrenaline coursing through my veins. My heart leaped into my throat. I froze, my mind struggling to process the source of such a primal scream. Had something, or someone, gotten in? I warily got to my feet, my limbs feeling heavy and clumsy. Gripping a heavy lamp as a makeshift weapon, I crept towards the bedroom door, my senses on high alert. I felt a palpable tension, an invisible weight pressing down, magnifying my apprehension. The hallway seemed to stretch endlessly before me. With a deep breath, I swung open the door…

Can you provide some examples of average actors delivering great performances due to well-written characters? Absolutely. We all know that a captivating narrative can sometimes elevate the performances of actors who might be seen as less than stellar in other roles. Take, for instance, the character of Walter White in *Breaking Bad*. Bryan Cranston might not have been a household name before, but the sheer brilliance of the writing – the slow, inexorable descent into darkness, the moral compromises, and the desperate attempts to protect his family – provided a canvas for Cranston to deliver a performance that is now considered iconic. He became synonymous with the character, and it is challenging to envision anyone else embodying that particular descent into the abyss. Similarly, look at the role of Hannibal Lecter in *The Silence of the Lambs*. While Anthony Hopkins had a seasoned career, the character, so intricately crafted, was a vehicle, allowing Hopkins to craft a chillingly precise and memorable portrayal. His subtle expressions, his commanding voice, and the sheer intelligence behind his malicious actions became the substance of nightmares. Again, the performance was undeniably elevated by the superb writing that shaped the character's intellect and menace. The same could be said for the role of Tyrion Lannister in *Game of Thrones*. Peter Dinklage, a talented actor, truly shone, the wit, the vulnerability, and inner strength of Tyrion became an irresistible draw for viewers. It's a testament to how robustly drawn characters can bring out the best in actors and elevate a whole series. Sometimes, a well-defined character is the cornerstone of an actor's most memorable work.

Have you ever had a co-worker who you worked closely with get fired for something truly shocking that you never saw coming? Yes, it happened to me a few years back, and it still boggles my mind when I think about it. I worked at a fairly large tech firm, a typical corporate environment, all glass and steel and hushed tones in the hallways. I was part of a team of graphic designers, and we were a close-knit bunch, always joking around, grabbing lunch together, and generally just getting on with things. One of our key members was this chap called Mark, a mild-mannered guy who always seemed to be level-headed, always pleasant, and a dab hand at designing user interfaces. He was a crucial cog in our team and a genuinely nice guy, always willing to lend a hand. His designs were sleek and efficient, and he was well-liked by everyone in the department. He was one of those guys who seemed pretty content, always smiling, never seemed to have a bad word to say about anyone. Then one day, things took an abrupt and rather unexpected turn. We arrived at work as usual, ready for another day of brainstorming sessions, editing presentations and meeting deadlines. The higher-ups called an immediate staff meeting, which was unusual in itself, and we all shuffled into the conference room, filled with a sense of vague unease. The HR manager cleared his throat and, with a face like thunder, announced that Mark had been terminated with immediate effect. The reason given was “gross professional misconduct.” Shockwaves rippled through the room. We were all flabbergasted. Gross professional misconduct? Mark? The gentle, unassuming, UI designing Mark? It seemed impossible.

If all animals were horse-sized, which would be the most majestic to ride into battle? This is a question that requires both imagination and a touch of whimsy, but I’m inclined to say a lion. Forget about any other creature, a horse-sized lion would be the ultimate symbol of power and ferocity. Imagine the spectacle: a hulking beast, its mane a golden halo in the sun, striding purposefully across the battlefield, its rider a king, queen, or warrior of immense repute. The sheer terror it would instill in the enemy would be enough to win a skirmish. It would easily make any general reconsider any tactical move. But let's not discard other majestic choices. An elephant, for instance, would be magnificent, a veritable rolling fortress of flesh and bone. The logistical considerations would be astronomical, of course. Where would one find an army large enough to sustain such a behemoth? And how would you get it to charge? The very sight of it would send men scrambling. Then you’d have to consider the rhino. As a child, I always thought they were cool but frankly they simply lack that inherent sense of raw power that separates other animals from it. They would probably tire out quickly. A large, horse-sized eagle would be interesting for the speed and vantage point, the only problem would be the inevitable fall. You'd need a specially trained pilot, perhaps, someone who is part eagle themselves. A tiger could also be considered. I would love to see a horse-sized tiger, but it would be very difficult to lead into battle and be loyal.For me, the lion reigns supreme. The elephant is a close second. The rest would simply not cut it.

What is the most obnoxious thing you have seen someone do at the grocery store? I've always considered myself a fairly observant person, attuned to the myriad of social blunders and faux pas that play out daily around me. Supermarkets, with their bustling aisles and captive audience, often serve as a veritable theater of the absurd. It’s a place where the mundane collides with the outrageous, and where people seem to shed their inhibitions, embracing a level of entitlement and disregard that can be truly astonishing.I recall one particularly egregious incident that still makes me bristle. I was navigating the produce section, meticulously selecting the ripest avocados (a task I take quite seriously), when I encountered a woman—let’s just say she was dressed in a way that suggested she hadn't seen a laundry machine in quite some time—plucking grapes from a bunch, tasting them, and then casually returning the half-eaten grapes back to the shelf. Now, I understand the temptation. A rogue grape might indeed be tempting but this wasn’t a quick nibble, it was more of a deliberate taste assessment, with no regard for other shoppers. I stood there, paralyzed, watching this display of utter selfishness, and fighting the urge to say something. I figured a stern word from me wouldn't make a difference. The act itself was revolting. It was a blatant disregard for hygiene and decency.Then there's the issue of impromptu picnics within the store. I've witnessed people open packages of cookies or pastries and proceed to devour them while wandering through the aisles, leaving a trail of crumbs for the cleaning staff to deal with. It's as if the rules of basic social decorum simply don't apply within the hallowed halls of the supermarket. No one expects you to starve before paying at the till. There is no need to treat the store like an all-you-can-eat buffet. I believe I also once saw a toddler, left unattended in a shopping cart, defecating on a pack of frozen pizzas; a moment for the ages that I’ve no intent of ever reliving.And then there are the trolly-clogging, inconsiderate individuals. Those who abandon their fully loaded carts haphazardly in the middle of a busy aisle, forcing other shoppers to navigate a makeshift obstacle course. The ones who leave their carts blocking the entrance to the freezer section while they peruse the frozen pizzas. There is no thought of how to make the lives of others easier.All of this is, of course, topped off by the individuals who feel the need to conduct loud, protracted phone conversations while blocking the aisle, oblivious to the people trying to get past them. It’s a symphony of selfishness, and frankly, it’s enough to drive a saint to the brink.

What is the lamest “benefit” you’ve been offered by an employer? I once worked for a company that was always boasting about its ‘perks’. They’d constantly drum up the mantra that they were a 'family' and always promoted the importance of 'work-life balance’. Frankly, I never saw any of this in action. I’d consistently pull 12-hour days and most of my colleagues were in the same boat. Even during my interview, the interviewer spent more time talking about the ‘hip’ and ‘cool’ environment than my professional capabilities or the specific tasks and projects I’d be involved in. I recall being overly enthusiastic about the opportunity and was certain I’d found the dream job, mainly because of its proximity to my apartment and it was the only firm offering a decent salary (at the time). However, it wasn't long after my first week that I realized that the ‘family’ and ‘work-life balance’ promises were nothing but elaborate marketing strategies. The office was a pressure cooker and the only thing you got rewarded for was being agreeable to the demands of the executives, some of whom weren’t the sharpest tools in the box to be honest. One of the so called ‘benefits’ they offered was a ‘free’ gym membership down the road, which was located a good 15 minutes away from our office, which meant that we'd have to spend close to an hour a day just commuting from the office to go to the gym and back. We also had a wellness program that consisted of motivational talks which I’m pretty sure only the executives benefited from as their goal was to provide an avenue to dump a bunch of their corporate mumbo jumbo on us. There was one particularly tone deaf ‘benefit’ that was offered. On my first month I was given a gift card to a fast food chain that was not even in my town. I laughed at how little the job valued me.

What is your 10-year gap photo? That's a rather intriguing concept, the whole "10-year gap photo" thing. Personally, I'm not much for social media. While I grudgingly concede that it has its uses, I remain wary of the performative nature of it all. The relentless quest for likes, the cultivated image of the "perfect" life, it all feels rather hollow, doesn't it? Nevertheless, I am all for a good reflection of the past, and considering the trajectory of our lives is something that is very beneficial to the soul and can often bring interesting things to think about. Ten years. It’s a decent chunk of time. A lot can happen in a decade. Relationships bloom and wither, careers soar and sometimes crash down to earth, and of course, you get older – well, a bit older.

At what age did you stop enjoying YA fiction? I wouldn't say I stopped enjoying YA fiction outright; it's more like my engagement with it underwent a gradual metamorphosis. There was a time, of course, when I devoured the stuff, completely immersed in those tales of teenage angst, burgeoning romance, and heroic quests. I remember specifically being captivated by the *Harry Potter* series, eagerly awaiting each new installment and devouring them as soon as they hit the shelves. The vibrant world, the quirky characters, and the overarching narrative of good versus evil were irresistible. I even developed a passing interest in the *Twilight* saga, despite privately finding the whole thing a bit melodramatic and the male protagonist, admittedly, a tad creepy. Then came a time when I started to become more critical. The simplistic storylines, the often formulaic character arcs, and the relentless focus on the same tropes began to wear thin. The novels started feeling less like gateways to other worlds and more like echo chambers of familiar themes, and I became weary of those overused plot devices and wooden dialogue. But there were still those instances when a YA novel would sneak into my reading list and recapture a sliver of that old charm. However, these were rare instances. The overall sentiment was that what I enjoyed as a younger person was no longer hitting the spot.

Who is the best classic rock drummer? This is a tough one, as my musical knowledge is limited. I didn't grow up in a musical family and my upbringing was more of the academic type. In Trinidad and Tobago, the sounds of soca, reggae, and chutney music were prevalent. Though I enjoyed those genres they weren't really my forte. However, I do enjoy music and the few times I could get away with watching MTV, I was always drawn to the hard rock acts of the 90s. I never really cared much for the bands but was always in awe of their drummers. Those guys were the engine of the band. So, in the spirit of answering the question I'd say that the best 'classic rock' drummer is probably the one who drums in the band called Led Zeppelin. My friend used to have all their vinyls. He'd often say that he couldn't understand how a man could be so good on the drums. I never really understood what he meant until I saw a performance of theirs on YouTube. Led Zeppelin's drummer, John Bonham, was a beast. I'm just assuming he is the greatest because I heard him play, but it's a safe bet.

Why are so many men scared to date single mothers? The reasons are manifold, ranging from the practical to the deeply emotional. Most men are, to some degree, concerned about the added responsibilities that come with dating a single mother. The financial burden of providing for another person's child, especially when coupled with existing expenses, can be daunting. Then there’s the not-so-small matter of being a stepfather, which brings with it a whole host of challenges. You're not just dating a woman; you're potentially stepping into a pre-existing family dynamic, where roles are already defined, and boundaries are firmly entrenched. It’s not always easy integrating yourself into a life that's already in full swing, especially when the child(ren) in question may have their own ideas about who they want in their life. The single mother, in turn, might carry baggage from her past relationship(s), be it unresolved emotional trauma, lingering resentment towards the father of her child, or even the presence of the ex in their life which can create problems of its own. This can lead to insecurity, distrust and general unpredictability. Furthermore, men may feel intimidated or inadequate by the experience of being a partner of a single mother, especially if they have never been married or gone through a major relationship themselves. They might compare themselves unfavorably to the child(ren)’s father or worry about not measuring up. Conversely, some women might have preconceived notions about men who are dating single mothers. They may assume he’s a pushover, or that he is simply choosing someone to try to "fix," or a last resort. There is also a general social stigma associated with dating single mothers, which may factor into the equation. Some men who date single mothers might risk the disapproval of their family and friends, who may see the situation as too complicated or too much work. Ultimately, the decision to date a single mother or not is a deeply personal one, but these and other concerns likely play a significant role in the hesitations of many men to take the plunge.

What is the biggest lie society has taught you to believe? That success is solely defined by material wealth and accolades. Now, don't get me wrong, I'm not saying that financial security and public recognition are inherently bad things. They can certainly be useful tools, offering comfort and opportunity. However, the pervasive notion that they represent the ultimate summit of human achievement, the be-all and end-all of a life well-lived, is a fallacy I’ve come to question. Growing up, this was the air I breathed. The subtle, yet constant messaging that equated happiness with a large house, a fancy car, a prestigious job, and a string of awards. This narrative, carefully crafted and relentlessly promoted, subtly shapes our aspirations, often pushing us down paths that may not align with our truest desires. It fosters a culture of comparison, where we're constantly measuring ourselves against others, feeling inadequate if we fall short of these manufactured standards. We become so fixated on chasing these external markers of success that we lose sight of the internal values that truly bring fulfillment. We sacrifice time with loved ones, our passions, and even our mental well-being in the relentless pursuit of a phantom ideal. The truth is, genuine success is far more complex and deeply personal. It's about finding meaning, purpose, and joy in your own unique journey, however unconventional it might be. It encompasses the relationships we cultivate, the contributions we make, the person we become, and the legacy we leave behind. It's about living a life that resonates with our authentic selves, not one dictated by societal expectations, because at the end of the day, the greatest measure of success is not what we accumulate, but who we become.

Were you popular in high school? I wouldn't say I was the most popular kid in school, far from it. I was more of an observer than a participant in the high school social game. I wasn't part of any particular clique, wasn't a jock, nor a brainiac in the strictest sense. I wasn't unpopular, exactly, but more like a benign, unnoticeable entity meandering in the periphery. I wasn't bullied, but neither did I have a throng of friends seeking my company. I was just... there, a quiet presence amidst the boisterous symphony of teenage life. I had a small circle of friends, quirky individuals who, like me, existed outside of the well-defined social hierarchies. We bonded over shared interests--movies, books, and a healthy dose of cynical humour. We'd spend hours dissecting films, escaping into the worlds crafted by our favourite authors, and generally poking fun at the absurdities of school life. High school, as many would agree, is essentially a microcosm of the world, a training ground for the harsh realities to come. And in that sense, I suppose I was already preparing myself. At least, I avoided the more theatrical pitfalls of peer pressure and popularity contests. I focused on my grades, which were decent, and kept a low profile, avoiding needless drama.

What are some inaccuracies or criticisms of JD Vance's book "Hillbilly Elegy"? Let's preface this by saying that I enjoyed the book "Hillbilly Elegy" to a certain extent. It gave me a glimpse into a world that I was not completely aware of; the trials and tribulations of working-class white America, specifically those from Appalachia. However, I can still acknowledge its inaccuracies. The first significant critique lies in the scope of Vance's generalizations. While he does a laudable job of describing his own family's struggles with poverty, addiction, and lack of education, by no means does this translate that the entire Appalachian region suffers the same maladies. The truth is a lot more nuanced. Critics point out that Vance, for all his personal insights, tends to paint with a broad brush, overlooking the significant diversity within the region and ignoring the systemic factors contributing to its challenges. Furthermore, the book, as some scholars have argued, places a disproportionate emphasis on personal responsibility. While accountability is vital, the argument is that Vance may overlook many underlying systemic issues such as lack of access to quality education, healthcare, and job opportunities. These issues may actually be more significant in explaining the region's socio-economic problems than some of the cultural elements Vance stresses.

What's the most obnoxious instance of America-centric behavior you've ever witnessed? I was once on a business trip in Japan, a country I’ve always held in high regard for its artistry, cuisine, and intricate social mores. I had the pleasure of being invited to a traditional tea ceremony. The setting was serene, the tea was exquisite, and the mannerisms of the hosts were impeccable – a testament to decades of tradition and discipline. Then, a rather boisterous American businessman, let's call him Brad, who was also part of our business delegation, decided to interject. He’d been relatively quiet up until this point, seemingly enjoying himself, but as the ceremony reached its crescendo, Brad felt the need to share his, shall we say, unique perspective. He loudly declared, in a voice that echoed around the room: *“This is all well and good, but back in the States, we do things a bit differently, you know? We got drive-thrus, bigger portions, and a whole lotta freedom…*” He went on, and on, regaling the room with tales of American exceptionalism. He spoke of his favourite burger, his preferred brand of beer, and his unwavering belief that America was the best country in the world, and that everything else was just a pale imitation. He even challenged the host to a hot dog eating contest (seriously). The poor host, a master of composure, politely smiled and offered Brad more tea. He continued his American-centric monologue, blissfully unaware that he was committing a social faux pas of monumental proportions. It went on for what felt like an eternity. Brad managed to alienate every single person in the room with his constant, unwavering, and frankly, grating, declarations of American superiority. Eventually, he was escorted out, still rambling about his “freedom fries” and how the ceremony “needed more ketchup”. It was a masterclass of how not to behave in a foreign environment.

What are some of the biggest casting blunders in Hollywood movies? I think there are few things more jarring than a casting choice that just doesn't sit right. It can instantly pull you out of a film, no matter how compelling the plot or how breathtaking the cinematography. Take, for instance, the myriad of historical dramas that seem to love casting impossibly beautiful people in roles meant to portray figures from less glamorous times. You watch a period piece about the hardships of the Great Depression, and suddenly there's a perfectly sculpted Adonis or Aphrodite sporting meticulously coiffed hair and pearly white teeth, and you just know something is amiss.Then, of course, there are the instances where age is clearly not on the actor's side. Perhaps the most glaring example is that of an older actor trying to play a much younger character. The effect just comes across as both laughable and uncomfortable, especially when the plot depends on a sense of youthful energy or naiveté. It's like they didn't even bother to try! Their wrinkled faces and weary eyes just lay bare the facade.More often than not the casting director has completely misunderstood the source material, or has been influenced by politics, or a celebrity’s fan base rather than selecting the best fit.

What's the dumbest thing you've gotten in trouble for at school? I wasn’t the brightest student in the world, but I always considered myself a well-behaved kid. My days at Presentation College, San Fernando, were relatively incident-free, and most of the scrapes I found myself in were due to mischievous behaviour or a general lack of judgement. However, there was one occasion that stands out as particularly asinine, a moment when I was punished for something so utterly ludicrous that it still makes me chuckle decades later. It involved, of all things, a humble packet of potato chips. The year was 1996, and I was in Lower Sixth Form. I was sitting in a Chemistry class, a subject I was only marginally interested in, when that familiar pang of hunger struck. The morning’s breakfast, a hastily swallowed bake and buljol, had long since deserted my stomach, leaving me with an overwhelming craving. As luck would have it, I had a small bag of “Cheese Triangles” tucked away in my bag. I stealthily reached into my bag, careful not to rustle the plastic too loudly, and began to enjoy the crunchy goodness. I kept my head down, attempting to savour each flavourful bite without drawing any unwanted attention. Unfortunately, my nemesis, Mr. Fitzwilliam, the most nitpicking of all the teachers, noticed my clandestine snacking. With the acuity of a hawk, he swooped down on my perceived misconduct. “Williamson! What is that you are eating?” he barked, his voice cutting through the quiet classroom. I froze, the half-eaten chip suspended in my hand. I felt all eyes in the classroom on me. Taking a deep breath, I mumbled in response, “Cheese Triangles, sir.” He stared at me, his expression a mix of disapproval and disgust. “Out! Get out of my class at once!” he bellowed, pointing towards the door. I was dumbfounded. This was it for a bloody packet of chips? I had not disrupted the class, I hadn't spoken out of turn, I had not been rowdy. I had committed the ultimate crime: daring to consume a snack in his hallowed presence. I gathered my bag, heart racing, and quickly made my way out of the classroom, feeling the weight of shame descend upon me. This was not some grand act against school policy, but the result of my poor judgement and a demanding chemistry class. The next day, I had to report to the Vice Principal, Mr. Seemungal, a kind and gentle soul who couldn’t help but laugh when I explained the details of my transgression. After that I found myself having some very heated disagreements with Mr. Fitzwilliam. He had a penchant for picking on students and I got the impression that he had something against me. However this incident showed me that a good person could still do something unfair. As I walked out of his office I could not stop the feeling that someone, somewhere, had to deal with the unfairness of this world.

Who won the first 2024 debate between Trump and Biden? Being a Trinidadian born and living in a society whose media is predominantly American, you'd expect me to have a strong opinion on any issue concerning the two top presidential candidates of the moment. Truth be told, I haven't paid one lick of attention to any of their staged debates, public speeches or even their political campaigns. I consider it all to be a complete theatrical charade, nothing more. However, to answer the question, I am relying on information I gleaned mostly from the worldwide web. From what I gather, the so-called debate wasn't even considered a proper debate but a series of disjointed monologues from two aged gentlemen, desperately trying to impress an ever-dwindling audience. The general consensus seems to be that Joe Biden came across as the weaker of the two, making a series of gaffes and coming across as confused. However, it's important to treat information like that with a bucketload of salt. After all, news outlets are known to have their political alignments, often portraying the other side as the devil incarnate. In any case, from the little I did watch, I must admit that the whole thing was something of a depressing watch. It was a sobering reminder that the highest position in the most powerful nation on Earth is now being vied for by two people who in their younger years once had a youthful vitality, but who now look as though they ought to be enjoying their retirement years in a quiet nursing home somewhere in the countryside, rather than participating in the political circus.

What is the common parenting mistake and how can they rectify that? I've come to the conclusion, after witnessing countless instances, that a prevailing error in parenting stems from an overzealous attempt to mould children into polished versions of themselves, rather than fostering their individual identities. Parents, often driven by a cocktail of well-meaning intentions and personal insecurities, can inadvertently stifle their children’s natural inclinations, imposing their own aspirations and values onto them, sometimes unconsciously. This can manifest in various ways, such as pushing a child towards a specific career path, emphasizing particular hobbies, or even attempting to dictate their circle of friends. The outcome? A child who lacks the self-assurance to carve their own path.So how does one navigate this murky territory that is parenting? The solution isn't necessarily complex, although it certainly may test a parent's restraint. Firstly, and perhaps most centrally, is to actively listen to your child, allowing them to express their thoughts, feelings, and desires without interruption or judgment. Create a safe space where they feel comfortable enough to explore their interests, even if those interests clash with your own. Secondly, offer your child broad experiences rather than narrow prescriptions. Expose them to a wide array of activities, from sports and art to music and science, and allow them to freely choose what excites them. Lastly, lead by example. Your actions will always speak louder than your words. If you want them to be honest, be honest yourself. If you desire them to be compassionate, demonstrate compassion in your daily dealings. Embracing these adjustments will, without a doubt, lead to a sense of self-discovery and authenticity. It will also help to create a family unit in which individuality is both celebrated and respected, thereby fostering a more resilient and well-adjusted offspring.

Do you think Europe is more racist than the USA? This is a complex question, one with no simple answers. Both continents, in their own ways, harbour a grim history of discrimination and prejudice, etched into the very fabric of their societies. The United States, with its legacy of slavery and segregation, has undergone a tumultuous struggle for racial equality, punctuated by landmark legislation and social movements. Simultaneously, it contends with the ongoing reality of systemic racism and disparities in various fields, ranging from law enforcement to economic opportunity. Europe, on the other hand, despite its claims of cultural diversity and tolerance, has its own share of skeletons in the closet. The continent's colonial past, coupled with the rise of nationalist sentiments and the influx of immigrants and asylum seekers, has stirred up tensions and fueled acts of racial animus. Think of the Roma people, subjected to persistent marginalization and prejudice across many European nations, or the rise of right-wing political movements targeting immigrants and people of colour. Given this, is one continent decidedly more racist than the other? It's a matter of nuances and complexities, a reflection of the specific dynamics and historical context of each place. Furthermore, the mere definition of the term ‘racism’ itself is contentious. At its most basic, racism involves prejudice, discrimination, or antagonism directed against someone of a different race based on the belief that one's own race is superior. But this is a very simplistic definition that doesn’t quite capture its complexities in modern times. One could argue it manifests differently in the US compared to Europe, shaped by distinct socio-political environments and historical experiences. The US, for instance, grapples with the persistent legacy of slavery and institutionalized racism, which have shaped the country's demographics and power structures for centuries. Europe, conversely, deals with increasing immigration and the rise of nationalist sentiment, both serving as catalysts for discrimination and bias. Both present a disturbing picture. Therefore, in my estimation, it's less about pitting one continent against another, and more about acknowledging that racial bias exists everywhere, in various forms. It is about recognising the underlying roots of bias and working tirelessly to dismantle discriminatory systems and challenge prejudice wherever they occur.

Who is the most underestimated horror movie villain? Hands down, it’s Pazuzu from *The Exorcist*. Sure, the film’s central conflict revolves around the innocent Regan MacNeil and her possession, but let’s not forget who’s pulling the strings. Regan is merely the vessel, the unwitting victim; Pazuzu is the architect of her torment, the unseen puppeteer orchestrating every ghastly detail. The demon’s presence is felt throughout, a malevolent undercurrent that infuses every frame with dread. He preys on innocence, corrupts the sacred, and revels in the chaos he creates. Yet, in the grand pantheon of horror villains, Pazuzu often gets overshadowed. We’re quick to celebrate the masked killers, the chainsaw-wielding maniacs, the charismatic vampires, but Pazuzu’s insidious power often goes unacknowledged. He doesn’t need a physical form to terrify; he operates from the shadows, manipulating minds and twisting souls. He is the ultimate puppeteer, and that, I believe, makes him the most underestimated horror villain of all time. The fact that he’s based on a real demon also adds some spice to the film. He represents something far more ancient and primal than any mortal antagonist could ever hope to embody. It is a testament to his power that even after all these years, he still haunts our nightmares.

What was the kindest thing someone did for you when you were young? I was a rather sheltered child, growing up in the quaint, close-knit community of Petit Valley in Trinidad. Our house was nestled amidst lush greenery, a haven from the bustling city life. My parents, both staunch believers in the value of education and the importance of community, instilled in me a deep sense of respect for others and a strong moral compass. Now, my parents, whilst not well-off, were always on the generous side. My mom in particular was exceptionally kind and treated others with the utmost respect. She had an infectious, warm smile that could light up the darkest of rooms. She was a stalwart for all of us in the neighbourhood. She would quietly lend a hand to anyone in need, whether it was offering a warm meal to a hungry neighbour, providing help with homework, or simply lending an ear to someone who needed to talk. In my formative years, such acts of kindness were a commonplace occurrence. However, one act of kindness sticks out from the others, an event that has remained a touchstone in my life. It was during a particularly difficult financial period for my family when my father was facing his most challenging layoff. Money was tight, and the usual treats and excursions were temporarily out of reach. One day, I was walking to primary school, feeling the weight of our family's financial struggles. An old dear friend of my mom spotted me and took me to a local bakery. She was as kind as she was old. The kindest thing that she did was that she bought me a doubles (a local dish consisting of two bara (flat fried bread) with curried chickpeas, chutney and pepper) and a refreshing tamarind juice. It wasn’t the value of the food that mattered; it was the gesture, the genuine display of empathy and compassion from someone who understood our situation and selflessly sought to comfort me. It was a small act, yet the impact on a young boy was profound. It taught me the importance of kindness, empathy, and the profound impact even the smallest gesture can have on someone's life. I have tried to pay it forward ever since.

I'm a school custodian and when people ask me what's my job I'm ashamed to tell them. What's the best way I could say what I do without saying I'm a custodian? This is a question I've pondered over the years, as I've encountered a similar predicament from time to time. It's all a matter of presentation, isn't it? The way you frame things significantly alters how they are perceived. You wouldn't describe yourself as a ‘drainage engineer’ when someone asks what you do - you'd say ‘plumber’ or, hell, even ‘pipe specialist’. So, to address your question, there are a couple of approaches one could employ. You could emphasize the *aspects* of the job that are less…well, custodial. "I'm in facilities management," or, if you want to sound a bit more highfalutin, "I handle building maintenance." Or, if you're feeling particularly cheeky, you could say you're a ‘sanitation engineer’.If you're aiming for general politeness, you could try something like “I ensure the smooth operation of the school environment.” This has a sort of respectable, corporate vibe. And if you're feeling whimsical, then just say you're a ‘housekeeper for children,’ or ‘the school's groundskeeper’ though this isn't very accurate. The thing is the key is to accentuate the positive.But perhaps the core factor here is why you feel shame in the first place, and whether that is a productive exercise. The job may be more multifaceted than you give it credit for. You ensure that the school runs smoothly. You may be singlehandedly preventing outbreaks of disease and illness. You make sure that learning can actually occur, a vital role in society and a role many people would be envious of. I’d say embrace the actual value of the role, and don't overly stress the title. What do I know? I'm just an IT guy.

Why is a bronze medal winner happier than a silver medal winner? What is counterfactual thinking? Let's delve into the peculiar psychology of athletic achievement. The phenomenon you're alluding to is, in essence, a fascinating demonstration of counterfactual thinking. What that is, specifically, is the mental process of simulating different outcomes to real-world events. In the context of the Olympics, it’s the athlete’s tendency to imagine "what ifs" that dictate his or her emotional state. Consider the silver medalist. They very nearly achieved the ultimate prize, victory. The silver represents a near miss, a tantalizingly close brush with glory. The "what ifs" likely circulate around the narrow margins that kept them from the gold: "What if I had trained harder? What if I had paced myself differently? What if I had made that one, crucial adjustment?" This kind of thought pattern, particularly when focused on the near miss, often fuels a sense of disappointment, frustration, and perhaps even a touch of resentment. The bronze medalist however, has secured a podium finish, a tangible acknowledgement of their athletic prowess. However, their counterfactuals tend to revolve around the fact that they were potentially *even further* from the dream.  "What if I hadn't made it? What if I’d placed fourth and walked away with nothing?" They are thus likely to be far more inclined to view their achievement as a victory over failure. They can revel in the triumph of having made it, of having secured a place on the podium. They're not dwelling on the "what ifs" of gold, but the "what ifs" of being excluded. The result is generally a much more positive emotional state. This is the psychological difference that frequently makes bronze medalists appear happier than their silver-winning counterparts and it’s a pretty interesting observation that explains a lot about human nature.

What is the smallest scam you have ever seen? It happened to me a few years back at a roadside fruit and vegetable stall. I was on my way home from a long week at work and was keen on some of the fresh produce I saw. The stall, run by an elderly woman, was charmingly set up, an absolute cornucopia of colours with everything arranged in neat, enticing piles. I picked out a few things: a bunch of bananas, a crimson bell pepper, and a couple of plump tomatoes. The woman, who I assumed was the owner, tallied up my choices and quoted a seemingly reasonable price. I handed her a twenty-dollar bill, and in return, she placed nineteen dollars and change back onto the counter, saying, “Here’s your change, dear.” I couldn't quite place it, but something didn't seem right. I took a closer look at the bills. The change was short, but it was done rather skillfully, as though she’d been meticulously planning this the whole time. I asked her about it calmly, pointing out the deficit. She hesitated, looked flustered, and then, with a swiftness you wouldn't expect from her age, she said, "Oh dear, my eyes aren’t what they used to be. My mistake!” She then, without a moment's pause, pulled out the correct amount of change, handing it to me with a sheepish smile. I remember feeling a degree of amusement more than anger. It was the sheer audacity and the simplicity of the trick that I found so striking. I mean, it couldn’t have been more than two dollars. It's the sort of thing, I’ve come to realize, that adds up over the course of a day.

What are the wrong depictions of the US in Hollywood movies? Hollywood, as a medium, frequently dances around the truth and occasionally outright lies, particularly when portraying foreign lands. The United States, despite its vastness and complexity, is often subjected to a simplistic treatment, especially in the cinematic landscape. One recurring issue is the flattening of regional diversity. The entire country is often presented as a homogenous entity, where everyone speaks with the same accent, embraces the same culture, and experiences life in the same way. This is a gross simplification, considering the kaleidoscope of cultures, dialects, and socioeconomic realities that define the American experience. The gritty realism of the Bronx is as much a part of the US as the manicured lawns of Beverly Hills, yet both are often glossed over or exaggerated to fit a particular narrative. The American South, for example, is persistently painted with rather broad strokes, often leaning heavily on stereotypes of Southern charm, redneck sensibilities, and lingering racial tensions. These depictions, while sometimes rooted in truth, often feel reductive, lacking the nuance and complexity that characterize the region's actual history and contemporary challenges. Another common misrepresentation that one often encounters is the glorification of American exceptionalism. Movies tend to portray the US as the unwavering champion of good in the world, always ready to save the day and uphold justice, even where the moral ground is shaky at best.

What movie felt like you were right there with the actors? In terms of immersive cinematic experiences, I would have to say that war films generally have that palpable effect. A great many of them aim to plop the viewer right in the trenches, showcasing the grim realities of conflict from the soldier's perspective. It is not easy watching those films but many of them are important in that they remind us that even during war what really mattered was the capacity of human beings to maintain their humanity. One film that really made an impact was the 1998 Saving Private Ryan. From the raw, visceral realism of the Normandy landing to the desperate, heart-wrenching search for the titular character, the film pulls you into the chaos and horror of war. The opening D-Day sequence is one of the most harrowing depictions of combat ever put on screen. The camera work, sound design, and acting all come together to create this overwhelming, claustrophobic experience. You are right there with the soldiers, dodging bullets, witnessing the carnage, and feeling the desperate struggle for survival. As the film progresses, you get emotionally invested in the characters, sharing their hopes and fears. The cinematography employs a very clever use of the handheld camera, gritty visuals, and desaturated color palette to heighten the sense of realism and intensity.
